Haplotype representation of the MHC region across apes

Source: vignettes/mhc-continuous-demo.Rmd
mhc-continuous-demo.Rmd

This tutorial first renders the complete MHC data object, then subsets it for a concise comparison. The remaining steps explain data composition, gene and lollipop layers, nucleotide links and the facet layout. The view recombines the gene identity and status information of Extended Data Fig. 3a/b with the continuous region and alignment design of Fig. 3c in Yoo et al. (2025). It is a source-backed reconstruction, not a pixel reproduction of the published figure.

Full MHC comparison

The complete source dataset contains 13 haplotype tracks: human CHM13 and both haplotypes of six ape species. Build and render the complete data object first. Run the code from a repository checkout root; these helpers are repository example functions, not exported package APIs.

library(ggexon)
source("data-raw/ape_paper/mhc_tutorial_data.R")

mhc_all <- read_mhc_data()
stopifnot(length(individual_names(mhc_all$species)) == 13L,
          nrow(mhc_all$mhc) == 285L)

mhc_all contains the SynSpecies object (species), native windows, MHC genes, context models, exons, variable regions and direct alignment tables. max_bp records the longest window in the complete dataset. The alignment collection contains the original 12 adjacent comparisons plus two direct bridges used by the later subset example; the full view draws only its 12 adjacent comparisons.

full_plot <- render_mhc_data(
  mhc_all,
  output_dir = "data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_full_example/figures"
)
full_plot$pdf  # exported vector figure

The full view below contains 285 curated MHC heads, the native-scale gene arrows and grey context genes, lower annotation lanes, and 624 nucleotide ribbons. Each track retains its native distances and assembly coordinate labels.

Subset the full data object

For a shorter example, retain human CHM13, both gorilla haplotypes and siamang h1. Gorilla’s two curated head profiles differ; siamang’s profiles match in gene identity, copy count, order, strand and status, so only one is shown. Human has only the CHM13 reference in these inputs.

keep <- c("SSYh1", "GGOh2", "GGOh1", "HSAh1")  # top to bottom
mhc_small <- subset_mhc_data(mhc_all, tracks = keep)

stopifnot(
  identical(individual_names(mhc_small$species), keep),
  length(pairwise_alignments(mhc_small$species)) == 3L,
  nrow(mhc_small$mhc) == 97L,
  identical(mhc_small$max_bp, mhc_all$max_bp),
  length(individual_names(mhc_all$species)) == 13L  # original unchanged
)

The subset retains the selected individuals with their attached annotations, filters every annotation table, keeps the direct alignments for adjacent selected tracks and rebuilds the chain layout. It preserves the full object’s max_bp and leaves mhc_all unchanged. The siamang h1 → gorilla h2 and gorilla h1 → human bridges were computed directly from the cached DNA, rather than inferred through removed tracks. A requested pair without a stored direct alignment raises an error.

compact_plot <- render_mhc_data(
  mhc_small,
  output_dir = "data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_compact/figures"
)
compact_plot$pdf

The concise view below has four annotation tracks, 97 MHC heads, 860 grey context arrows and 252 ribbons. It keeps the small native MHC arrows, six shared head rows, ortholog colors, pseudogene markings and lower annotation lanes. At 180 × 267.5 mm it is about 67% shorter than the full comparison.

Both examples use the same renderer. The following steps explain its data composition and layers. Full-dataset counts in these steps refer to the 13-track view. The website embeds verified previews because the source tables under data-raw/ are not installed with the package. Helper definitions are in data-raw/ape_paper/mhc_tutorial_data.R.

Step 1. What is in the MHC data?

All inputs are tab-separated tables under data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_continuous/. The main files are:

File One row per Key columns
windows.tsv haplotype window track, label, chr, start0, end0, length, orientation
gene_models_with_recovered_context/models.tsv representative transcript track, model_id, gene_symbol, chromStart, chromEnd, strand, annotation_evidence, projection_coverage, projection_identity
gene_models_with_recovered_context/exons.tsv supporting exon model_id, start0, end0
mhc_full/genes.tsv curated MHC gene track, locus, start, end, strand, gene_name, functionality
links.tsv alignment block tspecies, qspecies, tstart, tend, qstart, qend, strand, identity
discordant_regions.tsv variable-region piece track, region, start0, end0, display_start0, display_end0
source_metadata/mhc_continuous/colors.txt ortholog key gene key, RGB

Coordinate conventions matter here: windows.tsv and the derived tables use BED0, half-open coordinates (start0, end0). The curated genes.tsv table stores one-based closed coordinates (start, end), so the renderer converts start to start0 = start - 1 before plotting.

Representative rows look like this:

windows.tsv
track   label          chr             start0     end0       length    orientation
SSYh1   Siamang h1     chr23_hap1      37530567   42365376   4834809   -
PTRh1   Chimpanzee h1  chr5_hap1_hsa6  34745920   40035224   5289304   +
HSAh1   Human CHM13    chr6            28669878   33979214   5309336   +

genes.tsv
track   locus   start      end        strand  gene_name  functionality
HSAh1   MHC_I   29595529   29610626   +       HLA-F      functional

links.tsv
tspecies  qspecies  tstart  tend     qstart  qend     identity
SSYh2     SSYh1     1       113549   1       113407   97.9

The curated table has 285 records. functionality is the source call (functional or pseudogene); locus separates class I from class II; and gene_name supplies the identity key used for colors and for the shared head rows. The context tables contain released models and explicitly labelled same-species Liftoff projections, with annotation_evidence distinguishing the two.

B <- "data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_continuous"

windows <- read.delim(file.path(B, "windows.tsv"))
links   <- read.delim(file.path(B, "links.tsv"))
regions <- read.delim(file.path(B, "discordant_regions.tsv"))
models  <- read.delim(file.path(B, "gene_models_with_recovered_context/models.tsv"))
exons   <- read.delim(file.path(B, "gene_models_with_recovered_context/exons.tsv"))
mhc     <- read.delim("data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_full/genes.tsv")

Step 2. Data composition

Each track already has its own panel. facet_genomics() uses the panel’s x scale to position its data, and geom_nuclink() uses the corresponding source panel scales when placing ribbon endpoints. Panel limits handle fitting and zooming. A manual coordinate conversion is not required merely to display separate genomic panels.

This example’s preparation step brings its particular inputs into one consistent coordinate system:

Input Stored coordinates Composition for this example
Curated MHC gene spans One-based closed native assembly coordinates Convert to BED0, then express relative to the extracted window
Context models and VR intervals BED0 native assembly coordinates Express relative to the same window
Minimap2 alignment blocks Coordinates relative to extracted sequences Already window-relative; use the same convention as the gene layers
Siamang records Native assembly orientation is reversed Reflect gene and annotation coordinates to match the reverse-complemented alignment sequence

The gene tables and alignment tables must agree about what a position means. For this dataset, the renderer uses window-relative display coordinates. On a plus-oriented track it subtracts the window start; on a reverse-oriented track it reflects around the window end. These operations change the origin and orientation, not the genomic distances. Each row’s axis is labelled with its original native assembly coordinates at export.

The helper below shows that data preparation in the renderer. It is not an additional ggexon panel-fitting requirement:

transform_native <- function(d, a, b, trackcol = "track") {
  z  <- windows[match(d[[trackcol]], windows$track), ]
  lo <- pmax(d[[a]], z$start0)
  hi <- pmin(d[[b]], z$end0)
  d$xmin <- ifelse(z$orientation == "+", lo - z$start0, z$end0 - hi)
  d$xmax <- ifelse(z$orientation == "+", hi - z$start0, z$end0 - lo)
  d
}

Independent fitting and a common bp scale are different choices. If each panel fills the same width with its own complete region, a 4.83-Mb window and a 5.31-Mb window have different bp-per-mm ratios. That is a valid zoomed view. Here we keep one bp scale across haplotypes so expansions and deletions retain their relative sizes. The renderer therefore gives every panel the same display span, taken from the full object’s longest window:

max_bp <- mhc_all$max_bp
panel_xlim <- setNames(rep(list(c(0, max_bp)), nrow(windows)), windows$track)
panel_chr <- setNames(rep("MHC", nrow(windows)), windows$track)

The subset keeps this full-dataset span; it does not refit each retained region to occupy the full width. Translation/reflection composes the input coordinates; xlim and the panel scales control the view. Native coordinates could also be used directly if gene, annotation and link tables were all expressed in those same native coordinates.

The SynSpecies part is already assembled by read_mhc_data(). For the full view, retaining all track IDs selects its original 12 adjacent direct alignments and prepares the chain layout:

full_data <- subset_mhc_data(mhc_all, tracks = mhc_all$windows$track)
sp <- full_data$species
pair_names <- names(pairwise_alignments(sp))

Step 3. Genes first with geom_gene()

The first layer is the gene annotation. There are two kinds of arrows:

  • Context genes are representative source transcripts outside the curated MHC set. They are drawn in neutral grey with geom_gene().
  • Native MHC arrows are one small arrow per curated MHC gene, using the exact curated native span and the source ortholog color. They sit in the same lane as the context genes.

Neither layer draws exon glyphs: the transcript structure is used for model selection, but the figure shows one span per representative gene. Helper objects such as strip_labels, panel_limits and class_spans are built a few lines earlier in the renderer and omitted here so that the layer code stays readable. models and mhc in the code below are the transformed tables from Step 2 (the renderer calls the model table m), so their xmin and xmax columns are already display coordinates.

context_arrows <- data.frame(
  track = models$track,
  xmin = models$xmin, xmax = models$xmax, ymin = -0.5,
  transcripts = models$model_id,
  strand = models$strand,
  kind = models$kind
)

native_mhc_arrows <- data.frame(
  track = mhc$track,
  xmin = mhc$xmin, xmax = mhc$xmax, ymin = -0.5,
  transcripts = paste0("curated_native_mhc_", seq_len(nrow(mhc))),
  strand = mhc$display_oriented_strand,
  ortholog_fill = mhc$ortholog_fill
)

p <- ggexon(sp) +
  geom_gene(
    data = context_arrows,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, transcripts = transcripts,
        strand = strand, track = track, fill = kind),
    exon_height = 0.5, colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_gene(
    data = native_mhc_arrows,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, transcripts = transcripts,
        strand = strand, track = track, fill = I(ortholog_fill)),
    exon_height = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE
  )

xmin/xmax are display coordinates, ymin is the bottom of the gene lane, transcripts groups the rows, and strand controls the arrow direction. fill = I(ortholog_fill) bypasses the ggplot2 color scale, so each native arrow keeps the exact RGB value from colors.txt. The shared legend is supplied by the heads in the next step, not by this layer.

At this point p contains only the gene arrows: no heads and no ribbons.

Step 4. Add the MHC heads with geom_gene_lollipop()

Many MHC genes are only a few kilobases long, too small for a readable label at the native scale. The figure therefore adds one enlarged directional head per gene, anchored at the midpoint of the same curated span. The head is a fixed physical size; the small native arrow still carries the true span.

The curated table is extended with these plotting columns:

Column Meaning
true_midpoint midpoint of the curated span in display coordinates
display_oriented_strand strand flipped for a reverse-oriented track
gene_label source gene name, with * for a pseudogene
kind color/legend key (ortholog class, pseudogene, other gene)
head_row one of six shared physical rows for that source gene key

head_row is the key to the layout. Each of the 41 source gene keys is assigned a fixed row (1-6) from a template, so the same gene appears at the same height in every haplotype even when its native position differs. Distinct duplicated copies remain separate heads and are placed side by side on that row. An empty slot is a layout vacancy, not evidence that the gene is absent.

p <- p + geom_gene_lollipop(
  data = mhc,
  aes(x = true_midpoint, y = 0, strand = display_oriented_strand,
      label = gene_label, fill = kind, track = track, head_row = head_row),
  headroom = 8,
  head_layout = "columns",
  head_height_mm = 4,
  padding_mm = 0.6,
  tip_mm = 1.8,
  gap_mm = 0.8,
  row_gap_mm = 0.8,
  stem_height_mm = 1.5,
  family = "Times",
  size = 8 / ggplot2::.pt
)

y = 0 is the gene anchor line and headroom = 8 is the y-space above it that the heads may use. The *_mm arguments are physical sizes, not data units, so the heads stay legible when the figure is exported at 180 mm width. The stems rise from the exact midpoint ticks and fan into their columns; the layout is measured later and converted into panel heights.

Step 5. Connect haplotypes with geom_nuclink()

The last data layer is the nucleotide links. One geom_nuclink() call is added for each adjacent pair of haplotypes, using the stored SynPairAlignment:

for (nm in pair_names) {
  p <- p + geom_nuclink(
    alignment = nm,
    fill = "grey60",
    colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.3
  )
}

Each row of links.tsv is one ungapped alignment block: an interval on the target track (tspecies, tstart, tend) aligned to an interval on the query track (qspecies, qstart, qend), with strand and identity. The layer maps both intervals into the link panel between the two annotation rows and draws a quadrilateral (four vertices) for the block. In this figure there are 624 blocks across the 12 adjacent pairs, all drawn with the same grey fill and transparency.

The blocks were regenerated with minimap2 asm20 from the exact extracted native sequences, not taken from the unavailable original Fig. 3c plot data. Blocks are split at indels of at least 1 kb; blocks shorter than 500 bp or from parent alignments below 70% identity are omitted for display.

What the ribbons are - and are not

The ribbons are pairwise alignments, not a difference track. They show where two haplotype sequences align and where the alignment breaks. They do not measure base-level nucleotide differences, expression, or repeat copy number. identity is stored in the table and could be mapped to fill, but this figure keeps every ribbon grey.

If by “replica sequence” you mean duplicated or repetitive sequence: the links do not classify repeats. A tandem array or a duplication may produce repeated or non-colinear blocks, and an indel appears as a break between blocks, but that is an alignment pattern, not a repeat call. Repeats and segmental duplications need a separate annotation layer; they are not inferred from the ribbons.

Step 6. Tune the link panels with facet_genomics()

The script also adds the VR1-VR3 lane and the class I/II spans before faceting. They are ordinary annotations below the gene anchors:

p <- p +
  geom_rect(
    data = regions,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
    fill = "grey85", colour = NA, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = class_spans,
    aes(x = xmin, xend = xmax, y = y, yend = y),
    colour = "grey55", inherit.aes = FALSE
  )

The renderer computes the shared VR lane’s ymin and ymax from vr_top and vr_height; regions supplies the x intervals.

Faceting now creates one annotation panel per track and one link panel between each adjacent pair. The ratio between those two panel types is controlled by link_panel_height:

p <- p +
  facet_genomics(
    vars(track),
    scales = "free",
    ncol = 1,
    strip.position = "left",
    xlim = panel_xlim,
    xlim_chr = panel_chr,
    link_panel_height = 0.35,
    link_axis = "none",
    link_strip = "blank",
    labeller = labeller(track = strip_labels)
  ) +
  scale_panel_annotation("free_y", limits = panel_limits) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_family = "Times", base_size = 8,
                     show_x_grid = FALSE) +
  theme_ggexon_side_strips("left", base_size = 8)

link_panel_height is a relative height, not a millimetre value. A positive number is turned into a null grid unit relative to an ordinary panel row, so 0.35 makes each link panel roughly 35% of a standard annotation panel. Raise it when the ribbons are too flat to read; lower it when the links dominate the figure. Values around 0.2-0.5 are usually enough. The final export later fixes the link panels at 8 mm after measuring the heads, because the annotation panels shrink or grow around their labels.

scales = "free" frees the y range for each annotation panel. The x limits are still the same [0, max_bp] range on every track, so the base-pair scale stays common even though the facet is “free”; the per-panel y limits are supplied through scale_panel_annotation(). link_axis = "none" removes the axes from the link strips and link_strip = "blank" removes their strip labels. The left-side track labels come from theme_ggexon_side_strips().

Step 7. Measure the layout, fix the axes and export

The figure is 180 mm wide, but its height cannot be fixed in advance: each MHC head contains a label whose rendered width depends on the font and the number of columns. The renderer therefore draws the gtable once on a roomy 1000 mm PDF and records every head’s device position through the layout_callback of geom_gene_lollipop(). It then gives each annotation panel exactly the height its heads need and gives every link panel a fixed 8 mm.

Native axes are rebuilt in the same pass. The default bottom axis of each annotation panel is replaced with ticks in that track’s own one-based assembly coordinates; reverse-oriented tracks count down. Because the axis grobs are positioned through the shared display geometry, the tick spacing still proves the common base-pair scale.

built <- ggexon_build(p)
tab   <- ggexon_gtable(built)

# heads measured, panel heights assigned, native axes installed here

ggsave("mhc_continuous.pdf", tab, width = 180, height = measured_height_mm,
       units = "mm", device = cairo_pdf, bg = "white")
ggsave("mhc_continuous.png", tab, width = 180, height = measured_height_mm,
       units = "mm", dpi = 150, bg = "white")

The script fails loudly if the built object does not match the intended design. Its assertions and exported QC tables check, among other things:

  • 13 annotation panels, 12 link panels, no coverage panel;
  • one identical bp-per-axis-unit value across all annotation scales;
  • 285 heads at the true midpoints, with the recorded strand, label and row;
  • 624 ribbon blocks, four vertices per block, correct target/query ownership;
  • the shared VR lane, panel heights, figure dimensions and axis round-trips.

The QC outputs are written beside the figure as common-bp-scale-qc.tsv, native-geometry-qc.tsv, native-axis-qc.tsv, annotation-height-qc.tsv, link-qc.tsv, layout-qc.tsv and figure-dimensions.tsv, together with the plotted tables.

Gorilla class II detail

After composing the genes, heads, links and panel layout, the paired gorilla class II detail makes the h1/h2 differences easier to inspect:

Reading the figure

The small arrows retain each gene’s true curated span and source ortholog color; the enlarged heads carry the readable labels and direction on six shared rows. An empty head slot is a layout vacancy, not evidence that the gene is absent. Occupied slots are read top to bottom within a column, then left to right.

The grey VR1-VR3 bars are the published CHM13 variable-region intervals on the human track. On the ape tracks they show only the portions projected through human-to-ape chain blocks, so they describe shared comparative regions rather than independent ape-specific discordance. Asterisks mark pseudogene calls from the source annotation, not experimental validation.

Context layers labelled “projected” are same-species Liftoff transfers that passed at least 95% exon coverage and 95% sequence identity. Five alternative shorter isoforms were recovered at the same threshold; nine complete models remain unresolved. Recoveries use shorter source isoforms, and their RNA support is partial and not haplotype-resolved. Projected context is visualization context, not a complete validated alternate-haplotype gene catalog, and gene counts have different ascertainment across released and projected tracks. The region boundaries and adjacent alignments are documented reconstructions, not exact reproductions of the source figure.

Both versions are exported at 180 mm width, with height measured from the head layout. The original full vector PDF remains under data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_continuous/figures/; the compact version is under data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_compact/figures/ and is shown above.

Reproducing the compact and full figures

The compact example is reproducible from the whole data object with:

Rscript data-raw/ape_paper/render_mhc_compact.R

That entry point executes the same read → subset → render sequence shown above. It reads the checked-in compact direct-alignment table, so rendering does not require rerunning minimap2 or fetching DNA. Regenerating those alignments uses python3 data-raw/ape_paper/prepare_mhc_compact.py and requires the previously acquired regional FASTA caches and minimap2.

The original full view is displayed first above and is also available as the 13-track preview. Its bounded inputs and figure are under data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_continuous/. From the repository root:

Rscript data-raw/ape_paper/render_mhc_continuous.R

That command uses the final merged inputs and writes both figure formats and the QC tables. Rebuilding the inputs from raw sources additionally requires the bounded fetch, Liftoff projection, minimap2 and recovery steps documented in data-raw/ape_paper/results/mhc_continuous/README.md. data-raw/ is source material and is not installed with the package, so this vignette embeds the verified previews instead of re-running the source-data renderer during site builds.
